the association between sex specific BMI trajectories and the risk of incident HBP and HBG among Iranian adolescents to early adulthood.
the importance of the trend of BMI increase in adolescence and early adult years for the prediction of HPG and BP.
the association between BMI trajectories and incident HPG and incident HBP in a longitudinal cohort.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a higher BMI trajectory in adolescence to early adulthood is associated with higher risk of HBP and HBG.
overweight and obesity are risk factors for incident HBP and HBG.
overweight trajectories among males and overweight to early obese trajectories among females can be a risk for developing high blood pressure and plasma glucose.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the BMI trajectories can be used as a better predictor for HBP and HGP among females than males, and that among females, the trend of BMI increases can be a better indicator of risk than those with higher baseline BMI.
, for both sexes, the overweight trajectories are the most vulnerable for developing HBP, but only in females the overweight to obese trajectories are vulnerable for HPG.
overweight to early obese and overweight to late obese trajectories among females are associated with incident HPG and incident HBP, respectively.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, among adolescents, a trend of increasing BMI is a better predictor of HPG and BP than those with high BMI at baseline.
the trajectory of BMI is an important predictor of incident high BP and HPG, and the effect of BMI trajectory on HPG and HPG differs between males and females.
the trajectory of BMI change from early to late adolescence is a better indicator for future risk of HPG and BP than the BMI at a single time point.
